title: Exam technique: command words and timing
keyIdea: The command word tells you what kind of answer earns marks: describe says what happens, explain gives reasons, compare covers both things, and evaluate weighs both sides and then judges. The marks in brackets tell you how much to write and how long to spend, about a minute a mark on many papers. Mark schemes and past papers show exactly what earns each mark.

kid: Every exam question has a command word, such as describe, explain, compare or evaluate. It tells you the kind of answer that gets marks. A great answer to the wrong command word can still score low.

Describe means say what it is or what happens. Explain means give reasons, so use because and so. Compare means talk about both things and how they are alike or different. Evaluate means weigh up both sides, then make a judgement and say why.

Look at the marks in brackets. They tell you how many points to make and how long to spend. Work out the minutes per mark: time divided by marks. On many papers it is about a minute a mark. If you are stuck, flag the question, move on and come back.
Mark schemes show what examiners give marks for. Do past papers, then mark them with the scheme. You will see which points you missed, and why a long answer with no reasons can score zero.
adult: This topic covers how to read a question before answering it. Exam boards publish command words with set meanings. AQA, for example, defines explain as giving reasons, compare as setting out likenesses or differences rather than writing about only one thing, and evaluate as weighing evidence for and against to reach a judgement. The marks shown set how much is needed and how long to spend.

The lab works on five skills. Learners match four answers on one topic to the command word each one obeys. They upgrade a describe answer into an explain answer, and see that extra detail with no reason earns nothing. They share 45 minutes across six questions by marks, starting from an even split. They weigh points for and against before choosing a justified judgement, and mark three answers against a mark scheme.

The most common mistake is answering the topic and not the command word: describing when asked to explain, or writing about one thing when asked to compare. Another is ending an evaluate answer with no judgement, or a judgement with no reason. Learners also give every question the same time, or spend far too long on a low-mark question they are stuck on.
At home, pick a past paper question and ask your learner to circle the command word and say what it wants before writing. Then mark the answer together with the published mark scheme.

familyTip: Before your teen answers a past paper question, ask them to circle the command word and say what it wants, then work out the minutes from the marks. Afterwards, mark it together with the published mark scheme.

practice.prompt: A question says: Describe the pattern in the graph. Which answer does what it asks?
choices: Sales rose each year, fastest in 2021
Sales rose because prices fell
Electric cars are better than petrol cars
practice.hint: Describe asks what happens, not why or which is better.
practice.explain: Describe means say what the pattern is. Giving reasons is explain, and choosing a winner is evaluate.

practice.prompt: A paper lasts {=3*m} minutes and has {=2*m} marks. About how many minutes should a {=2*h}-mark question get?
practice.hint: First find the minutes per mark: time divided by marks.
practice.explain: {=3*m} ÷ {=2*m} = 1.5 minutes per mark, so {=2*h} marks get 1.5 × {=2*h} = {=3*h} minutes.

practice.prompt: Explain why ice melts faster in a warm room. [2 marks] Which answer earns both marks?
choices: It melts faster because the air is warmer, so heat moves into the ice faster
It melts faster in a warm room
Ice is frozen water and it melts
practice.hint: Explain needs a reason. Look for because and so.
practice.explain: The first answer gives a reason and its effect. The others only say what happens or state a fact.

practice.prompt: A question is worth {m} marks. You have spent {=3*m} minutes on it and you are stuck. What is the best move?
choices: Flag it, move on and come back at the end
Keep going until you get it
Leave it blank for good
practice.hint: How much time is it worth? What else could those minutes earn?
practice.explain: At about a minute a mark, {m} marks are worth about {m} minutes, and {=3*m} is far more. Move on and come back.

practice.prompt: Compare the two cities. Which sentence is a comparison?
choices: City A is larger, whereas City B is older
City A is large and busy
I would rather live in City B
practice.hint: A comparison must talk about both things.
practice.explain: Compare needs both: whereas links a point about A to a point about B. A preference is not a comparison.

pool.prompt: What does evaluate ask you to do?
choices: Weigh both sides, then make a judgement with a reason
Describe what happens in detail
List as many facts as you can
pool.hint: How does an evaluate answer end?
pool.explain: Evaluate means weigh evidence for and against, then decide and say why. A description alone has no judgement.

pool.prompt: What does explain ask you to do?
choices: Give reasons why something happens
Say what something looks like
Write about only one side
pool.hint: Which small words show a reason?
pool.explain: Explain asks for reasons: because, so, which means. Saying what something looks like is describe.

pool.prompt: A paper has {m} marks and lasts {=m+5} minutes. You keep 5 minutes to check. How many minutes should a {q}-mark question get?
pool.hint: Take off the checking time, then divide the minutes by the marks.
pool.explain: {=m+5} − 5 = {m} minutes for {m} marks is 1 minute per mark, so {q} marks get {q} minutes.

pool.prompt: An evaluate answer lists four good points for school uniform and stops. What is missing?
choices: The other side and a final judgement
More detail on the four points
A diagram
pool.hint: Evaluate weighs both sides. Did it?
pool.explain: It needs points against and a judgement with a reason. More detail on one side still never evaluates.

pool.prompt: Why mark your past paper answers with the mark scheme?
choices: It shows exactly which points earn marks and which you missed
It is the same as reading the textbook
It tells you your final grade
pool.hint: What does a mark scheme list?
pool.explain: The scheme lists the points examiners reward, so you can see which ones your answer missed.

pool.prompt: A question is worth {m} marks. How many separate points does it usually need?
choices: About {m}, one per mark
Just 1, however long
As many as you can fit
pool.hint: Look at the number in brackets.
pool.explain: Points-based questions often give one mark per point, so {m} marks usually need about {m} clear points.

pool.prompt: Six questions share 40 minutes. Q1 is 2 marks and Q6 is 12 marks. How should you split the time?
choices: About 2 minutes on Q1 and 12 on Q6
The same time on each
Most time on Q1 because it comes first
pool.hint: Should time follow the marks or the order?
pool.explain: Time should follow the marks: about a minute a mark, so 2 minutes for Q1 and 12 for Q6.

pool.prompt: Before writing, what is the first thing to do with a question?
choices: Find the command word and the marks
Start writing everything you know
Skip to the hardest question
pool.hint: What tells you the kind of answer and how long to spend?
pool.explain: The command word says what kind of answer earns marks, and the marks say how much and how long.

visual.caption: Which answer does the command word want? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: The graph rises, then levels off
The leaf is broad and flat
The leaf is broad so it catches more light
It melted since the room was warm

lab.caption: Flagship lab: match answers to command words, upgrade an answer to earn its marks, plan minutes by marks, weigh then judge, and mark like an examiner.
